## Background

In March 2020, as COVID-19 lockdowns shut businesses across the United States, Congress created the Paycheck Protection Program (PPP) under the CARES Act. The idea was simple: give small businesses low-interest loans to keep paying their staff, and forgive the loan entirely if the money went to payroll and other eligible costs. The program eventually grew to around [\$800 billion](https://files.gao.gov/reports/GAO-25-107267/index.html).

Speed was the priority. Loans were processed by private lenders, often within days, and borrowers largely self-certified their eligibility, payroll and number of employees. That design got money out quickly, but it also made the program an easy target. In June 2023, the SBA's Office of Inspector General [estimated](https://www.hsgac.senate.gov/subcommittees/etso/hearings/examining-federal-covid-era-spending-and-preventing-future-fraud/ware-testimony) that more than \$64 billion in PPP funds went to potentially fraudulent actors. The SBA [disputed](https://meritalk.com/articles/sba-oig-potentially-fraudulent-covid-loans-topped-200b/) the size of that estimate, but even its own figures pointed to tens of billions of dollars needing investigation.

With hundreds of thousands of loans and limited investigators, the practical question is not "which loans are fraudulent?" but "which loans should be looked at first?". A spreadsheet cannot prove fraud. What it can do is surface patterns that fraud tends to leave behind, known as red flags, so investigators spend their time on the most suspicious cases.

That is what this analysis does. I take the SBA's public data on every PPP loan over \$150,000, define a set of red flags grounded in the program's rules, score each loan against them, and test whether flagged loans were more likely to end up charged off. The aim is triage, not accusation: a flag means a loan deserves a closer look, not that the borrower did anything wrong.

## Data

Loan-level data comes from the U.S. Small Business Administration's [PPP FOIA dataset](https://data.sba.gov/dataset/ppp-foia) (public domain). This analysis uses the file of loans of \$150,000 and over (`public_150k_plus_240930.csv`).

```{r libraries}
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
library(knitr)
```

```{r load-data}
ppp <- read_csv(
  here::here("data", "ppp", "public_150k_plus_240930.csv"),
  na = c("", "NA", "N/A"),
  col_types = cols(LoanNumber = col_character())
) |>
  mutate(across(c(DateApproved, LoanStatusDate, ForgivenessDate), mdy))
```

The file contains `r format(nrow(ppp), big.mark = ",")` loans and `r ncol(ppp)` columns, approved between `r format(min(ppp$DateApproved, na.rm = TRUE), "%d %B %Y")` and `r format(max(ppp$DateApproved, na.rm = TRUE), "%d %B %Y")`.

## Exploratory data analysis

### Data quality

Before defining any red flags, I checked the fields the flags will depend on: where the borrower is located and how many jobs they reported.

```{r missing-values}
ppp |>
  summarise(
    `Borrower state missing` = sum(is.na(BorrowerState)),
    `Project state missing`  = sum(is.na(ProjectState)),
    `Both missing`           = sum(is.na(BorrowerState) & is.na(ProjectState)),
    `Jobs zero or missing`   = sum(is.na(JobsReported) | JobsReported == 0)
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "Check", values_to = "Loans") |>
  kable(format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

The data is close to complete on these fields. Only a handful of loans are missing a state or a job count, out of almost a million, too few to affect the results, so I leave them as missing rather than trying to fill the gaps. One cleaning step mattered more: some missing values are stored as the text "N/A" rather than left blank. Left as-is, every loan with an "N/A" address would look like it shared one address, creating a fake cluster of borrowers.

### Loan outcomes

The data has no column that says "this loan was fraud". The closest thing is the loan's final status.

```{r loan-status}
ppp |>
  count(LoanStatus, sort = TRUE) |>
  mutate(Share = scales::percent(n / sum(n), accuracy = 0.1)) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Loan status", "Loans", "Share"),
        format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

Almost all loans were paid in full, which for PPP mostly means forgiven: `r scales::percent(mean(!is.na(ppp$ForgivenessAmount[ppp$LoanStatus == "Paid in Full"])), accuracy = 0.1)` of paid-in-full loans have a forgiveness amount recorded. A small share were charged off, meaning the lender gave up on recovering the money. A charge-off does not prove fraud, since a genuine business can fail, but fraudulent loans are far more likely to end this way because the borrower never intended to repay or apply for forgiveness. I use charge-offs as a stand-in outcome to test whether the red flags carry real signal.

The third status, "Exemption 4", refers to the Freedom of Information Act exemption for confidential commercial or financial information. The SBA withheld these loans' status under it, a decision [upheld in court](https://infobytes.orrick.com/2021-12-17/district-court-grants-sbas-summary-judgment-covid-19-relief-disclosure-case/) after lenders said they treat loan status as confidential.

### Business age

To be eligible, a business had to be [in operation on 15 February 2020](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2020-04-15/html/2020-07672.htm). Borrowers described their business age on the application, so this field is a natural place to look for ineligible loans.

```{r business-age}
age_outcomes <- ppp |>
  filter(LoanStatus != "Exemption 4", !is.na(BusinessAgeDescription)) |>
  group_by(BusinessAgeDescription) |>
  summarise(Loans = n(),
            `Charged off` = sum(LoanStatus == "Charged Off"),
            `Charge-off rate` = mean(LoanStatus == "Charged Off")) |>
  arrange(desc(Loans))

age_outcomes |>
  mutate(`Charge-off rate` = scales::percent(`Charge-off rate`, accuracy = 0.1)) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Business age", "Loans", "Charged off", "Charge-off rate"),
        format.args = list(big.mark = ","))

rate <- function(age) {
  scales::percent(age_outcomes$`Charge-off rate`[age_outcomes$BusinessAgeDescription == age], accuracy = 0.1)
}
startup <- age_outcomes |> filter(BusinessAgeDescription == "Startup, Loan Funds will Open Business")
```

New businesses (two years old or less) were charged off at `r rate("New Business or 2 years or less")`, more than double the `r rate("Existing or more than 2 years old")` rate for established businesses. That makes sense: a young business has less trading history for a lender to check. Still, more than 96% of new-business loans ended paid in full, so on its own this is a weak signal. It is more useful combined with other flags.

Borrowers who left the question unanswered were also charged off more often than established businesses, at `r rate("Unanswered")`.

The most striking category is "Startup, Loan Funds will Open Business". Taken literally, a business that will open with the loan money was not operating on 15 February 2020 and should not have qualified. But only `r startup$Loans` loans fall in this group, and `r startup$"Charged off"` of them were charged off, a rate close to established businesses. With so few loans the rate is unreliable, and the label may not mean what it says for every borrower. I treat it as a flag worth checking by hand rather than proof of ineligibility.
 These loans are not known to be clean, just unknown, so I leave them out when comparing flagged and unflagged loans.
